newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Nations meet to help build Bosnian police force.
newsitem.headline: Nations meet to help build Bosnian police force.

text.p: Officials of more than 30 countries met in Dublin on Saturday at a United Nations conference aimed at raising $99 million to help to build a democratic police force in post-war Bosnia.

Several countries promised to consider providing money for the project, but few made any immediate pledges. The main financial contribution came from the United States, which announced a package worth $17 million.

Peter Fitzgerald, head of the U.N. International Police Task Force (UNIPTF) which is overseeing the transition to a democratic civilian police force in Bosnia, said he was not disappointed with the immediate response.
"Nobody can be disappointed when they're offered $17 million cash up front and then other assistance after that," he told reporters after the conference.

"This was the first opportunity we have had to meet the international community and let them see what we are doing, what we have achieved in the past and what we hope to achieve in the future. I think they will come back with considerably more, having considered that."

At the conference, U.N. officials and representatives from Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and the Bosnian Serbs discussed the resources and training needed to build an effective democratic police force.
Jock Covey, chief of staff at the office of the U.N. High Representative in Sarajevo, said a viable police force was vital to the creation of democracy after years of war.

"No peace process has ever before attempted such a comprehensive restructuring of police functions. And perhaps police functions have never been closer to the heart of a peace process," he told the conference.
"Until recently, many police were armed elements of the warring factions. They also have a long history as guardians of an authoritarian state," Covey said.

"My simple message to you today is that the police in Bosnia must become part of the solution -- not part of the problem. If not, none of the other investments we are making to consolidate peace in this region can be fully realised."
Kofi Annan, U.N. Under-Secretay General for Peacekeeping Operations, said the cost of training and equipping the police force would be around $99 million.
"The task ahead of us is enormous," he said. "It is vital and it will require material and financial support."
Annan said the conference was a first step in winning international financial support for the new police force.
"We will follow up again and again in the hope that your governments will make a contribution to make this endeavour possible," he told delegates. "Without it we will not be able to proceed." REUTER
